# Osteoporosis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Endocrinology > Bone and mineral disorders > Osteoporosis*

[Original Article Link](/library/cT0ap2)

---

## Summary

Osteoporosis is a skeletal condition in which the loss of <u>bone mineral density</u> (<u>BMD</u>) leads to decreased bone strength and increased susceptibility to <u>fractures</u>. <u>Postmenopausal</u> women and older adults are often affected, as an abrupt decrease in <u>estrogen</u> and age-related processes play a key role in the development of osteoporosis. Additional <u>risk factors</u> include physical inactivity, a diet low in <u>calcium</u> and <u>vitamin D</u>, smoking, and <u>alcohol</u> consumption. Osteoporosis usually remains asymptomatic until the first occurrence of a <u>fragility fracture</u> (typically following minor trauma). Patients may also present with thoracic <u>hyperkyphosis</u> and height loss secondary to multiple <u>vertebral compression fractures</u>. Diagnostic evaluation includes <u>BMD assessment</u> (e.g., <u>dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry</u>), <u>fracture</u> risk assessment, and workup for common causes of <u>secondary osteoporosis</u>. <u>Fractures</u> are usually confirmed through <u>conventional x-ray</u>. Pharmacotherapy is indicated in patients who fulfill the <u>diagnostic criteria for osteoporosis</u>. <u>Bisphosphonates</u>, which inhibit bone resorption and can significantly decrease the risk of <u>fractures</u>, are the preferred first-line treatment. Nonbisphosphonates are indicated in patients who are unable to take <u>bisphosphonates</u> and those in whom <u>bisphosphonate</u> therapy has been unsuccessful. Prevention mainly comprises of adequate <u>calcium</u> and <u>vitamin D</u> intake and <u>regular physical activity</u> with strengthening exercises to maintain or even increase <u>bone mass</u> and improve balance, thereby reducing the risk of falls and <u>fragility fractures</u>. High-risk individuals should be offered <u>screening for osteoporosis</u> and pharmacotherapy should be initiated in those with <u>osteopenia</u> at a high risk of <u>fractures</u>.

---

## Definitions

* Osteoporosis: loss of trabecular and <u>cortical bone</u> mass which leads to bone <u>weakness</u> and increased susceptibility to <u>fractures</u>

* Osteopenia: decreased bone strength but less severe than osteoporosis

---

## Epidemiology

* Sex: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (∼ 4:1)

* Age of onset: 50–70 years

* Demographics: higher <u>incidence</u> in individuals of Asian, Hispanic, and northern European ancestry [[1]](/library/_fX5Kx)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

### Primary osteoporosis (most common)




* Type I (postmenopausal osteoporosis): <u>postmenopausal</u> women [[2]](/library/WQWPEO0)[[3]](/library/SQWyvO0)

* <u>Estrogen</u> stimulates <u>osteoblasts</u> and inhibits <u>osteoclasts</u>.

* The decreased <u>estrogen</u> levels following <u>menopause</u> lead to increased bone resorption.

* Type II (senile osteoporosis): gradual loss of <u>bone mass</u> as patients age (especially > 70 years)

* <u>Idiopathic</u> osteoporosis

* <u>Idiopathic</u> juvenile osteoporosis  [[4]](/library/K2XUix)

* <u>Idiopathic</u> osteoporosis in young adults  [[5]](/library/62Xjix)





### Secondary osteoporosis




* Drug-induced/<u>iatrogenic</u>

* Most commonly due to systemic long-term therapy with <u>corticosteroids</u> (e.g., in patients with autoimmune disease)  [[3]](/library/SQWyvO0)

* Long-term therapy involving: [[6]](/library/hQWcDO0)

* <u>Anticonvulsants</u> (e.g., <u>phenytoin</u>, <u>carbamazepine</u>)

* <u>L-thyroxine</u>

* <u>Anticoagulants</u> (e.g., <u>heparin</u>)

* <u>Proton pump inhibitors</u>

* <u>Aromatase inhibitors</u> (e.g., <u>anastrozole</u>, <u>letrozole</u>)

* <u>Immunosuppressants</u> (e.g., <u>cyclosporine</u>, <u>tacrolimus</u>)

* <u>Androgen deprivation therapy</u> (<u>ADT</u>)

* Endocrine/metabolic: <u>hypercortisolism</u>, <u>hypogonadism</u>, <u>hyperthyroidism</u>, <u>hyperparathyroidism</u>, renal disease

* <u>Multiple myeloma</u>





### Additional <u>risk factors</u>  [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)




* <u>Excessive alcohol consumption</u>

* <u>Cigarette smoking</u>

* <u>Immobilization</u> or inadequate physical activity

* <u>Malabsorption</u> (e.g., <u>celiac disease</u>), <u>malnutrition</u> (e.g., diet low in <u>calcium</u> and <u>vitamin D</u>), <u>anorexia</u> [[8]](/library/IUXYex)

* Low body weight

* <u>Family history</u> of osteoporosis

* Personal history of <u>fracture</u>

---

## Clinical features

* Mostly asymptomatic

* Fragility fractures: <u>pathological fractures</u> that are caused by everyday-activities (e.g., bending over, sneezing) or minor trauma (e.g. falling from standing height) [[9]](/library/3QWSDO0)

* Common locations of major osteoporotic fractures: <u>vertebral</u> (most common) > femoral neck > <u>distal</u> radius (<u>Colles fracture</u>) > other <u>long bones</u> (e.g., <u>humerus</u>)

* <u>Vertebral compression fractures</u>  

* Commonly asymptomatic but may cause <u>acute back pain</u> and possible point tenderness without neurological symptoms

* Multiple <u>fractures</u> can lead to decreased height and thoracic <u>kyphosis</u>.

* See “<u>Vertebral fractures</u>” for more information.





![Compression fractures of the vertebra](media/o4a52mkts41vtemechwno79e.jpg)

Compression fractures of the vertebra

---

## Screening

### Indications [[10]](/library/xJdEwI0)




* Screening is recommended in:

* Women ≥ 65 years of age

* <u>Postmenopausal</u> women < 65 years of age with ≥ 1 <u>risk factor for osteoporosis</u>

* Individuals with a history of low-trauma <u>fracture</u> after 50 years of age [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)

* There is insufficient evidence to recommend routine <u>screening for osteoporosis</u> in men; consider screening: 

* Younger men with <u>risk factors for osteoporosis</u> (e.g., long-term <u>corticosteroid</u> use; <u>ADT</u> for <u>prostate cancer</u>) [[12]](/library/4sX3Ez)[[13]](/library/3k1SnS0)

* Men ≥ 70 years of age [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[12]](/library/4sX3Ez)[[14]](/library/CHXqsz)





> [!TIP]
> The majority of screening and prevention recommendations are for women; consult an endocrinologist for men with suspected osteoporosis.




### Modality [[10]](/library/xJdEwI0)




* ≥ 65 years of age: <u>BMD assessment</u>; <u>DXA</u> of <u>lumbar spine</u> and hips is preferred. [[10]](/library/xJdEwI0)[[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[15]](/library/Y41n3S0)

* < 65 years of age

* <u>Stratify</u> patients using an osteoporosis risk assessment tool, e.g., <u>FRAX</u>.

* For patients with a clinically significant risk of osteoporosis, obtain <u>BMD assessment</u>.





### Further management




* If the <u>diagnostic criteria for osteoporosis</u> are fulfilled, start <u>treatment for osteoporosis</u>.

* For all other patients:  [[16]](/library/9wcNOe0)

* <u>Optimize bone health</u> and discuss fall prevention.

* For high-risk individuals : Start <u>pharmacotherapy for osteoporosis prevention</u>. [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)

* Reassess <u>BMD</u> at regular intervals.

* There is a paucity of data on the value and optimal timing of repeating the <u>BMD assessment</u>.

* Determine the need for and frequency of screening intervals on an individual basis based on the initial <u>BMD</u> (<u>T-score</u>) and development of new <u>risk factors for osteoporosis</u> or <u>fractures</u>.





| <br>Suggested frequency of <u>osteoporosis screening</u> [[16]](/library/9wcNOe0)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| <br><u>T-score</u><br>(in SD)<br> | Intervals |
| -2.0 to -2.4 | within 3 years<br> |
| -1.5 to -1.9 | 3–5 years |
| -1.0 to -1.4 | 5–10 years |
| > -1.0 | > 10 years |





> [!WARNING]
> Short-interval (within 2–3 years) reassessment of <u>BMD</u> in individuals who do not fulfill the <u>diagnostic criteria for osteoporosis</u> is not routinely recommended. [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[16]](/library/9wcNOe0)

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)




Osteoporosis is typically identified during screening in high-risk individuals (see “<u>Screening for osteoporosis</u>”).




* Assess <u>BMD</u> and estimate the risk of <u>major osteoporotic fracture</u>.

* The diagnosis is confirmed if any of the following diagnostic criteria for osteoporosis are fulfilled. [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)

* <u>T-score</u> ≤ -2.5 standard deviations (SDs) on <u>dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry</u> (<u>DXA</u>)

* <u>T-score</u> -1 to -2.5 SD in patients at increased risk of <u>major osteoporotic fracture</u>

* History of a <u>major osteoporotic fragility fracture</u> (regardless of <u>BMD</u>)

* Once confirmed:

* Consider screening all patients for common causes of <u>secondary osteoporosis</u>.

* Evaluate high-risk patients for <u>vertebral fractures</u>.

* Consider <u>bone turnover markers</u> (<u>BTMs</u>) to assess <u>fracture</u> risk and monitor treatment response.





> [!TIP]
> Osteoporosis is diagnosed in patients with a <u>T-score</u> ≤ -2.5 SD and/or a <u>fragility fracture</u>. [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)




### Bone mineral density (BMD) assessment [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[15]](/library/Y41n3S0)




#### Indications




* Evaluation of suspected osteoporosis

* <u>Screening for osteoporosis</u> in asymptomatic high-risk individuals





#### Preferred modality: dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry




<u>DXA</u> measures <u>BMD</u>;  at the <u>lumbar spine</u> and hip/femoral neck using two <u>x-ray</u> beams.  Findings are represented in terms of <u>BMD scores</u> that compare results to a reference population.




| <br>BMD scores [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[15]](/library/Y41n3S0)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Postmenopausal</u> women and men > 50 years of age | <br><br>* <u>BMD</u> is calculated using the T-score.<br><br>* <u>T-score</u> ≤ -2.5 SD indicates osteoporosis [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[15]](/library/Y41n3S0)<br><br>* <u>T-score</u> -1 to -2.5 SD indicates <u>osteopenia</u> [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[15]](/library/Y41n3S0)<br><br>* <u>T-score</u> ≥ -1 SD is normal [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[15]](/library/Y41n3S0)<br><br><br> |
| All other individuals | <br><br>* <u>BMD</u> is calculated using the <u>Z-score</u>.<br><br>* <u>Z-score</u> < -2 indicates <u>BMD</u> likely lower than expected for age [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[15]](/library/Y41n3S0)<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> <u>DXA</u> evaluates bone quantity. The <u>trabecular bone score</u> uses data from <u>DXA</u> images to evaluate bone quality and may sometimes be used to further <u>stratify</u> <u>fracture</u> risk. [[17]](/library/zwcrle0)




![DXA scan in osteopenia](media/jrs9ppcrptguddirpxra1rjr.jpg)

DXA scan in osteopenia




#### Alternatives [[15]](/library/Y41n3S0)




These studies are most commonly used when conventional <u>DXA</u> is unavailable.




* Peripheral <u>DXA</u>: measures <u>BMD</u> at the <u>distal</u> forearm

* Quantitative computed tomography

* Provides a volumetric measurement of <u>BMD</u> at the <u>lumbar spine</u> and hip

* Can measure density of <u>trabecular bone</u>

* May be superior to <u>DXA</u> in patients with: [[15]](/library/Y41n3S0)

* Very tall or very <u>short stature</u>

* Significant <u>degenerative disk disease</u>

* <u>BMI</u> > 35 kg/m<sup>2</sup>

* Close monitoring of <u>trabecular bone</u> density changes (e.g., chronic <u>glucocorticoid</u> use, <u>parathyroid hormone</u> therapy)





### <u>Fracture</u> risk assessment [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)




* Several calculators are used to estimate <u>fracture</u> risk during the diagnostic workup or <u>screening for osteoporosis</u>.

* FRAX (commonly used; see “Tips and Links”): estimates the 10-year <u>probability</u> of a <u>major osteoporotic fracture</u>   [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[14]](/library/CHXqsz)





### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)




Consider screening all patients with newly diagnosed osteoporosis for common causes of <u>secondary osteoporosis</u> and potential contraindications for certain pharmacotherapy.




* Routine studies

* <u>CBC</u>, <u>CMP</u>, <u>PTH</u>, <u>phosphate</u>, and serum <u>25-hydroxyvitamin D</u>

* 24-hour urine to measure <u>calcium</u>, <u>creatinine</u>, and <u>sodium</u> levels

* Additional studies 

* Evaluate for specific etiologies of <u>secondary osteoporosis</u> as guided by clinical assessment (e.g., <u>celiac antibodies</u>, <u>TSH</u>, myeloma screen).

* Consider <u>BTMs</u> to assess <u>fracture</u> risk and monitor treatment response. [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[18]](/library/jsX_uz)

* Findings

* <u>Primary osteoporosis</u>: Serum <u>calcium</u>, <u>phosphate</u>, and <u>parathyroid hormone</u> (<u>PTH</u>) levels are usually normal

* <u>Secondary osteoporosis</u>: See “<u>Laboratory findings in common bone disorders</u>” and/or relevant articles for details.





> [!TIP]
> Treat <u>vitamin D deficiency</u> and ensure at least 2 weeks of recommended daily intake of <u>calcium</u> before obtaining 24-hour urine <u>calcium</u>. [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)




### Screening for <u>vertebral fractures</u> [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[15]](/library/Y41n3S0)[[19]](/library/FHXgHz)[[20]](/library/zHXrGz)




<u>Vertebral fractures</u> are common in patients with osteoporosis, asymptomatic in up to two-thirds of cases, and associated with a high risk of future <u>fractures</u>.




* Indications: <u>T-score</u> ≤ -1.0 in individuals with one or more of the following [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[19]](/library/FHXgHz)

* Women ≥ 70 years of age or men ≥ 80 years of age

* Height loss of ≥ 4 cm (> 1.5 inches)

* Undocumented (self-reported) prior <u>vertebral fracture</u>

* <u>Kyphosis</u>

* Recent long-term <u>glucocorticoid</u> therapy

* Modalities [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[15]](/library/Y41n3S0)

* Vertebral fracture assessment (<u>VFA</u>): uses <u>DXA</u> to assess for <u>vertebral fractures</u>

* <u>Lateral</u> thoracic and <u>lumbar spine</u> <u>x-ray</u>

* Supportive findings (on <u>x-ray</u>)

* Increased <u>radiolucency</u> and cortical thinning  [[21]](/library/Z9cZNe0)

* <u>Vertebral compression fractures</u>





![Decreased bone density in osteoporosis](media/s3zi7swj899xxis97glfa5xq.jpg)

Decreased bone density in osteoporosis

![Thoracic wedge compression fracture](media/kg6kfmly5zj1mstukrbvekc5.jpg)

Thoracic wedge compression fracture

![Chronic lumbar compression deformity](media/ct09d0m6ftpjripr52hf50i0.jpg)

Chronic lumbar compression deformity

![Acute and chronic vertebral fractures](media/i9hpnvt6g71vprbkt85eh7rx.jpg)

Acute and chronic vertebral fractures




### Imaging for other skeletal <u>fractures</u> [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[22]](/library/N2X-3x)




* Indications

* Symptoms of <u>fracture</u> (e.g., <u>pain</u>, limited mobility)

* Thigh or groin <u>pain</u> in patients on long-term (∼ 5 years) <u>bisphosphonate</u> therapy  [[23]](/library/DHX1sz)

* Modalities

* First line: <u>plain x-ray</u>

* Second-line : Consider <u>MRI</u> or CT.

* Supportive findings

* <u>Radiographic signs of a fracture</u>

* Atypical femoral fractures: Transverse noncomminuted <u>fracture</u> of the subtrochanteric region or shaft of the <u>femur</u>  [[24]](/library/RsXluz)

* Increased <u>radiolucency</u> (on <u>x-ray</u>/CT) and cortical thinning  [[21]](/library/Z9cZNe0)





![Bisphosphonate-related atypical femoral fracture](media/tde9tcp4b8qkh1ztec2nx0lm.jpg)

Bisphosphonate-related atypical femoral fracture

![Chalkstick fracture](media/lcotlf3poddiar4hpb8vqf3v.jpg)

Chalkstick fracture

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Osteomalacia</u>

* <u>Hyperparathyroidism</u>

* <u>Metastases</u>

* <u>Multiple myeloma</u>

* <u>Intraosseous hemangioma</u>





![Thoracic vertebral hemangioma](media/hu8nz8a97x5tbmo3ljxc01ei.jpg)

Thoracic vertebral hemangioma

![Intraosseous hemangioma in the lumbar vertebrae](media/mcxrof3m9damgkywwenc8gso.jpg)

Intraosseous hemangioma in the lumbar vertebrae




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

## Treatment

### Approach [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)




* All patients: <u>Optimize bone health</u>.

* Older patients: Assess for and manage <u>risk factors</u> for falls. [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[25]](/library/Q2duh60)

* Discuss fall prevention strategies.

* Identify and manage <u>risk factors</u> for falls using the <u>CDC STEADI algorithm for falls</u>.

* Recommend individual and/or group exercise interventions that incorporate strength and balance training.

* Refer to physical and/or <u>occupational therapy</u> as needed.

* Start pharmacotherapy in the following situations:

* <u>Diagnostic criteria for osteoporosis</u> fulfilled

* Patients with <u>osteopenia</u> at increased risk of <u>major osteoporotic fracture</u> in the next 10 years

* See also “<u>Introduction to geriatrics</u>” for general information on the <u>prevention of falls in older individuals</u>.





### Pharmacotherapy for osteoporosis [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[26]](/library/WXWPCP0)[[27]](/library/6Hdjrr0)




#### Indications [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)




* Treatment: patients who fulfill any of the <u>diagnostic criteria for osteoporosis</u>

* Prevention: patients with <u>osteopenia</u> and an increased <u>probability</u>   of a <u>major osteoporotic fracture</u> in the next 10 years (as determined on a clinical risk assessment tool such as the <u>FRAX</u>)





#### General principles [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)




* <u>Bisphosphonates</u> are preferred first-line agents.

* Consider nonbisphosphonates as first-line alternatives in certain situations or as second-line agents if <u>bisphosphonate</u> therapy is unsuccessful or not tolerated.

* Combination therapy with agents of different classes is currently not recommended.

* Agents approved for osteoporosis treatment in men [[12]](/library/4sX3Ez) 

* Alendronate, risedronate, <u>zoledronic acid</u>, and <u>teriparatide</u>

* <u>Denosumab</u> is approved for men receiving <u>ADT</u> for <u>prostate cancer</u>.

* Agents approved for glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[28]](/library/I41YkS0)

* <u>Bisphosphonates</u>, <u>denosumab</u>, and <u>teriparatide</u>

* <u>Teriparatide</u> may be more effective at preventing <u>vertebral fractures</u> in this patient group than the other agents.





#### Bisphosphonates for osteoporosis [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)




* Indications: : preferred initial treatment in all patients   [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[23]](/library/DHX1sz)[[28]](/library/I41YkS0)

* Mechanism of action: inhibition of <u>osteoclasts</u>, which are involved in bone resorption

* Agents: The following are approved for both prevention and <u>treatment of osteoporosis</u>.

* Alendronate DOSAGE [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)

* Risedronate DOSAGE [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)

* Ibandronate (only <u>FDA</u>-approved for <u>postmenopausal</u> women) DOSAGE [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)

* <u>Zoledronic acid</u> DOSAGE [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)

* Adverse effects [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[29]](/library/L2XwRx)

* <u>Osteonecrosis of the jaw</u>

* <u>Atypical femoral fractures</u>

* <u>Esophagitis</u>

* <u>Hypocalcemia</u>

* See also “<u>Contraindications to bisphosphonate therapy</u>” and “<u>Duration of pharmacotherapy for osteoporosis</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> Oral <u>bisphosphonates</u> should be taken in the morning with plenty of water at least 30 minutes before food and other medication, and the patient should maintain an upright position for at least 30 minutes after intake to prevent <u>esophagitis</u>. [[14]](/library/CHXqsz)




> [!TIP]
> Alendronate, risedronate, and <u>zoledronic acid</u> reduce hip, <u>vertebral</u>, and nonvertebral <u>fracture</u> risk; ibandronate reduces <u>vertebral fracture</u> risk only. [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)




#### Nonbisphosphonates [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[23]](/library/DHX1sz)




* General indications

* Alternative first-line agents in patients with <u>contraindications to bisphosphonate therapy</u>

* Second-line agents in those who do not improve with <u>bisphosphonates</u>  or are unable to tolerate <u>bisphosphonate</u> therapy (e.g., due to adverse effects)

* Specific indications: detailed below





| <br>Nonbisphosphonates for the treatment of osteoporosis [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[23]](/library/DHX1sz)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | <br>Specific indications [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[12]](/library/4sX3Ez)<br> | Mechanism of action | Potential adverse effects |
| <br>DenosumabDOSAGE [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)<br> | <br><br>* Patients with impaired renal function<br><br>* Men undergoing <u>ADT</u> for <u>prostate cancer</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Monoclonal antibody</u> against the <u>receptor</u> activator of nuclear factor-κB <u>ligand</u> (<u>RANKL</u>)<br><br>* Targets <u>RANKL</u> by mimicking <u>osteoprotegerin</u> → interference in <u>osteoclast</u> maturation → ↓ <u>osteoclast</u> activity [[30]](/library/zsXrxz)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Hypocalcemia</u><br><br>* <u>Osteonecrosis of the jaw</u> (uncommon)<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>PTH</u> and <u>PTH-related protein</u> analogues <br><br>* Teriparatide DOSAGE [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)<br><br>* Abaloparatide DOSAGE [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)<br><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Alternative for patients at high or very high risk of <u>fracture</u><br><br>* <u>Teriparatide</u>: Treatment of <u>glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis</u>  [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[28]](/library/I41YkS0)<br><br><br> | <br>* Recombinant human <u>parathyroid hormone</u> that increases <u>osteoblastic</u> activity → increased bone growth [[31]](/library/aGXQBz)[[32]](/library/cGXayz)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Hypercalcemia</u> (usually transitory)<br><br>* <u>Dizziness</u>, <u>hypotension</u><br><br>* <u>Tachycardia</u><br><br>* Muscle spasms<br><br>* Use with caution in patients with <u>risk factors</u> for <u>osteosarcoma</u>, e.g.:<br><br>* <u>Paget disease of the bone</u> (or unexplained elevation of <u>alkaline phosphatase</u>)<br><br>* Prior cancer or <u>radiation therapy</u> of the bone<br><br>* Open <u>epiphyses</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Romosozumab DOSAGE [[33]](/library/0GXeBz)<br> | <br>* Alternative for <u>postmenopausal</u> women with multiple <u>vertebral fractures</u> or very high <u>fracture</u> risk<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Monoclonal antibody</u> against sclerostin<br><br>* Acts by increasing bone formation and reducing bone resorption<br><br><br> | <br>* Avoid in patients at increased risk of cardiovascular disease, as <u>romosozumab</u> may increase the risk of:<br><br>* <u>Myocardial infarction</u><br><br>* <u>Stroke</u><br><br>* Cardiovascular <u>death</u><br><br> |
| <br>RaloxifeneDOSAGE [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)<br> | <br>* Can be used in patients at increased risk of <u>breast cancer</u>  [[34]](/library/M_cMKU0)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Selective estrogen receptor modulator</u> (<u>SERM</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Increased risk of <u>venous thromboembolism</u><br><br> |
| <br><u>Calcitonin</u> DOSAGE [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Postmenopausal osteoporosis</u> (rarely used because of the availability of more effective alternatives) [[33]](/library/0GXeBz)<br><br>* A short course may be prescribed for <u>acute pain</u> caused by <u>vertebral fractures</u>  [[35]](/library/R9clMe0)<br><br><br> | <br>* Inhibits bone resorption (monitor <u>BMD</u>) [[36]](/library/nGX7-z)<br><br> | <br>* May increase overall cancer risk [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)<br><br> |
| Hormonal therapy | <br><br>* <u>Estrogen</u> (women): not approved for <u>osteoporosis treatment</u>   [[23]](/library/DHX1sz)<br><br>* <u>Testosterone</u> (men): used to treat low <u>testosterone</u> levels in men with <u>hypogonadism</u>  [[12]](/library/4sX3Ez)<br><br><br> | <br>* Inhibits <u>bone remodeling</u> [[37]](/library/MGXM-z)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Estrogen</u> therapy is associated with an increased risk of:<br><br>* <u>Thromboembolism</u><br><br>* <u>Stroke</u><br><br>* <u>Myocardial infarction</u><br><br>* Certain cancers (e.g., <u>breast</u>, <u>endometrial</u>, ovarian)<br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Estrogen</u> is not approved for the <u>treatment of osteoporosis</u> in women; if <u>estrogen</u> is prescribed to a patient with a <u>uterus</u>, it should always be combined with <u>progesterone</u> therapy to reduce the risk of <u>endometrial hyperplasia</u>. [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[23]](/library/DHX1sz)

### Monitoring and follow-up [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[14]](/library/CHXqsz)[[23]](/library/DHX1sz)




* Regularly review patients to assess for problems with adherence; see “<u>Managing chronic conditions</u>.”

* Consider <u>BTMs</u> to assess treatment <u>efficacy</u> and adherence. [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)

* Measure height yearly; if there is a ≥ 2 cm height loss, repeat imaging for <u>vertebral fractures</u>.

* Obtain <u>DXA</u> every 1–2 years for patients on treatment to monitor response. [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)

* Markers of improvement: stable or increasing <u>BMD</u>, no new <u>fractures</u>, normal or low <u>BTMs</u>

* If there is inadequate improvement : [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz) 

* Consider alternative agents or reevaluate for <u>secondary osteoporosis</u>.

* Consider referral to a clinical endocrinologist or osteoporosis specialist, if available.





| <br>Duration of pharmacotherapy for osteoporosis [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Duration of therapy | Additional considerations |
| <u>Bisphosphonates</u> | <br><br>* Insufficient data on optimal duration<br><br>* Consider discontinuing <u>bisphosphonates</u> after 5 years in women with no history of <u>vertebral fractures</u>. [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)<br><br>* In patients at very high risk of <u>major osteoporotic fractures</u>, consider a total duration of:<br><br>* 10 years for oral <u>bisphosphonates</u><br><br>* 6 years for <u>zoledronic acid</u> in patients<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Bisphosphonates</u> can be discontinued temporarily (“<u>bisphosphonate</u> holiday”) after 3–5 years of treatment.<br><br>* Optimum duration of <u>bisphosphonate</u> holiday is unclear: Monitor <u>BMD</u> using <u>DXA</u> regularly and restart treatment if <u>BMD</u> declines or if the patient sustains a <u>fracture</u>.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Abaloparatide</u>, <u>teriparatide</u> | <br>* 2 years<br><br> | <br>* Transition to <u>bisphosphonates</u> or <u>denosumab</u> after discontinuation.<br><br> |
| <u>Romosozumab</u> | <br>* 1 year<br><br> |  |
| <u>Denosumab</u> | <br>* Indefinite<br><br> | <br>* Transition to another antiresorptive agent.<br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> The benefits of nonbisphosphonates are lost rapidly after discontinuation; initiate another <u>treatment for osteoporosis</u> after cessation. [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[14]](/library/CHXqsz)

## Prevention

### General measures [[7]](/library/Z41Z3S0)[[14]](/library/CHXqsz)




* Optimize <u>calcium</u> and <u>vitamin D</u> intake. 

* Recommended daily intake of <u>calcium</u>: 1000–1200 mg  [[14]](/library/CHXqsz)

* Recommended daily intake of <u>vitamin D</u>: 800–1000 IU  [[14]](/library/CHXqsz)

* <u>Treat vitamin D deficiency</u>.

* Encourage physical activity, including strength (resistance) and balance training.

* Avoidance or minimization of the following:

* Tobacco use: See “<u>Counseling on smoking cessation</u>.”

* <u>Excessive alcohol consumption</u>: See “<u>Counseling on alcohol abuse</u>.”

* <u>Glucocorticoid</u> use; see also “<u>Measures to prevent complications of steroid therapy</u>” [[38]](/library/PsXWEz)





### Pharmacotherapy for osteoporosis prevention [[39]](/library/iFXJ3-)




* Indication: individuals with <u>osteopenia</u> who are at high risk for osteoporotic <u>fractures</u>  [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)

* Preferred agents: <u>bisphosphonates</u> (see “<u>Bisphosphonates for osteoporosis</u>” for dosages) [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)

* Alternatives for <u>postmenopausal</u> women in whom <u>bisphosphonates</u> are inappropriate  or who desire pharmacotherapy for <u>management of menopause</u> symptoms  [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)[[40]](/library/rbXfE9)[[41]](/library/WeXPBC)

* <u>Raloxifene</u> DOSAGE [[11]](/library/_HX5Gz)

* Consider <u>estrogen</u>  or conjugated <u>estrogen</u>/bazedoxifene; see “<u>Hormone replacement therapy</u>” for dosages and details.
